absent: Low-level frame remapping installer behavior beyond delegation, including tracking variants and failure modes.
File offset resolution and flag mask values used during remap preparation.
IO remap preparation and installation semantics and their locking.
Page table allocation, lookup, and synchronization helpers and architecture sync mask.
Consumption of the fault-around window during fault handling.
Frame-map argument structure definition and caller lock holding durations.
Remote page pinning, stack growth helpers, and area access hooks.
String length limits and IO-backed string copy handling.
Page table lock usage and descriptor layout.
Memory policy modes, enforcement, and weighted interleave computation.

findings.text: Public remap entries prepare a virtual area for frame-backed mapping and then delegate to a lower-level installer. Preparation derives an aligned end, resolves copy-on-write status, computes a file offset for the range, and applies a fixed remap flag mask before delegating. A completion variant draws start address, base frame, length and protection from a pending action record and delegates identically.

Simple IO mapping preparation validates a physical range against a virtual length and offset, converts the accepted range to a starting frame number, records a full IO mapping action, and then runs IO remap preparation. A virtual-area variant performs the same validation using the area length and its start offset, then installs the mapping with the area protection.

Physical range validation rejects address-plus-length overflow and frame-plus-page-count overflow, tolerates unaligned physical starts by widening length down to page alignment, shifts the start by the requested page offset with rejection when the offset exceeds available pages, and rejects virtual lengths that do not fit the remaining pages, signalling all failures with an invalid-argument error.

Page range application walks page tables from the top level down to entries and invokes a caller callback once per entry in the interval. One entry point creates missing intermediate tables while walking, and a second entry point visits only already-present tables and skips absent subtrees.

The walk rejects empty or wrapped ranges, rejects huge leaf entries encountered at intermediate levels, skips malformed entries when only visiting while reporting and clearing them when creating, reports allocation failures as out-of-memory and missing or leaf cases as invalid-argument, stops at the initial callback failure, and requests kernel mapping synchronization when the accumulated modification mask intersects an architecture-defined set.

At the entry level the walk uses kernel-only allocation and lookup paths for the initial address space and locked map-and-hold paths otherwise, enables deferred flush mode around the callback loop, marks entries modified, and releases the entry lock with unmapping for non-initial spaces. When only visiting, absent entries are skipped and the callback runs solely on populated entries.

Malformed upper-level entries are handled by emitting a table error diagnostic and then clearing the entry, which confines corruption handling to the affected slot during creating walks and avoids dereferencing invalid descriptors.

Fault-around window state is a page count whose byte view is the count shifted by page size. The default count equals 65536 [CITED] scaled down by page size. Updates reject counts above entries per table, clamp small values up to a single page, and round down to a power of two before storing as pages.
An initialization routine publishes the fault-around byte control as a debug filesystem file with mode 0644 [CITED], backed by get and set handlers described elsewhere.

The frame-map lookup result carries a held lock, an optional mapped entry pointer, a resolved frame number, an alignment mask, a protection value, and writable and special flags, together with the target area and address supplied by the caller. Setup derives the frame by adding the masked address offset in pages to a level base frame.
Frame-map lookup requires address space locking: file-backed areas must hold either the mapping lock or the address space read-write lock, while anonymous areas must hold the address space lock.

Frame-map lookup validates that the address lies inside the area and that the area carries IO or frame-map flags, then descends through successive table levels with lockless reads. Huge leaves are locked and revalidated with a retry when the level changed concurrently, ordinary entries are mapped and locked, populated state is required at each stage, and any failure yields an invalid-argument error. A paired release unlocks the held lock and unmaps the entry pointer when present.

The successful lookup returns holding the table lock for the leaf level, either a huge-level lock with no mapped entry or an entry lock with a mapped pointer, and ownership transfers to the caller until the paired release runs.

Physical access snapshots protection, frame and writability from an initial lookup, checks write intent against writability, maps the covering pages with the snapshotted protection, revalidates against a second lookup and retries from the start on any change, then copies between kernel IO mapping and caller buffer in the requested direction and returns the transferred length.

Remote address space access takes a killable read lock, removes tagging from the address, ensures a backing area with stack growth handling, and iterates page by page. Pinned pages are mapped locally with partial-page bounds, copied in the requested direction with dirty marking on writes, while unpinnable IO areas fall back to area-specific access hooks when available. The routine releases the lock and returns bytes moved.

Stack growth drops the read lock and acquires a killable write lock, re-resolves the area and predecessor, succeeds immediately when the address already lies inside an area, otherwise attempts upward growth of the predecessor and then downward growth of the successor, downgrades to a read lock on success, and unlocks with failure when neither direction grows.

Upward and downward growth availability is build-dependent: one configuration grows upward and fails downward growth, while the alternate configuration grows downward and fails upward growth, with the unsupported direction reporting a fault error.
Without virtual memory management, stack growth never succeeds and only releases the read lock before reporting failure.

Remote string copy NUL-initializes the destination, handles empty lengths and missing address spaces distinctly, and otherwise copies a NUL-terminated string page by page with local mappings, stopping at the terminator or the length bound and preserving the trailing byte when crossing page boundaries, returning bytes produced or a fault error.

Diagnostic printing of the area owning an instruction address uses a non-blocking read-lock attempt and silently returns under contention, making it safe from atomic context. When the area exists and is file-backed, it reports the caller prefix with file identity and offset-adjusted position plus area bounds, then releases the lock.

Fault-allowance checking returns immediately when faults are disabled, otherwise records a potential sleep point and, when a user address space is present, performs a read-lock state check on its address space lock.
The folio zeroing locality radius equals 2 [CITED].

A copy argument bundles destination and source folios with a virtual area. Per-subpage copying addresses matching indices in both folios and maps machine-check copy failures to a hardware-poison error while reporting success otherwise.

A dedicated slab cache holds page table locks. Initialization creates the cache with panic-on-failure semantics, allocation draws a lock and attaches it to the descriptor reporting success or failure, and freeing releases the attached lock when present.

Internal migration flags derive from a shared internal base shifted left by 0 [CITED], 1 [CITED] and 2 [CITED] to respectively allow discontinuous ranges, invert node-mask matching, and write-lock walked areas.

Policy infrastructure keeps separate slab caches for policies and shared nodes, a zero-initialized zone selector, a permanently referenced local default policy, a per-node preferred policy table, a reference-counted weighted-interleave state with an automatic mode flag plus a flexible weight table, and a node bandwidth table.
The fixed interleave weightiness equals 32 [CITED].
A dedicated mutex serializes updates to the weighted-interleave state.
Memory policy logging prefixes messages with the module name.
